html:
The map's label for early maize-growing peoples outside the heartland of Mesoamerica, shown from 1500 BCE to 200 BCE.

Maize was first bred in south-western Mexico from a wild grass, teosinte, by the early farmers of Mesoamerica. From there it spread north and south over thousands of years. It reached the deserts of the American Southwest by about 2000 BCE, where farmers in the Tucson area were digging irrigation canals by about 1200 BCE, and it spread through Central America and into the Andes.

Early maize farmers rarely lived on maize alone. They still hunted and gathered, and grew squash and beans alongside. Over time, larger cobs and methods such as nixtamalisation made maize a staple. In the Southwest these farmers were forerunners of the Hohokam and their neighbours, while the desert foragers around them kept a hunting and gathering life.
